title: Reading application and system logs
description: Find and interpret Linux logs to understand what happened in production.

data.text: Logs are the primary record of what happened on a Linux server. System logs record kernel events, service startups, and authentication attempts. Application logs record what your software was doing when it worked, failed, or slowed down. Learning to read logs efficiently is one of the highest-value troubleshooting skills.
Logs are often the only evidence left after a crash. If you know where to look and how to filter, you can reconstruct events, find the root cause, and prevent the problem from recurring.

items: /var/log/syslog or /var/log/messages: system-wide logs on Debian/Red Hat

data.text: On systems using systemd, journalctl is the preferred way to read logs. It can show logs for a specific service, time range, or priority level. It also has powerful filtering options that make it faster than grepping flat files.

data.code:
journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago"
journalctl -p err -b     # errors since last boot
journalctl -f             # follow logs in real time

data.text: Application logs vary in format: plain text, JSON, or structured logs. The key is to identify the error pattern. Use grep to find error lines, tail to see the most recent entries, and awk or sed to extract fields. If logs are structured, jq is invaluable for querying JSON logs.

data.code:
tail -n 100 /var/log/app/app.log | grep ERROR
grep -c "timeout" /var/log/app/app.log
journalctl -u myapp --since "yesterday" | grep -i failed

data.title: Log levels
data.text: Logs typically use levels: DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, and FATAL. When diagnosing, start with ERROR and FATAL. WARN can show early signs of trouble. DEBUG is noisy but useful if you can reproduce the issue.

Production issues often involve multiple services. A slow request might start in nginx, pass through an API server, and fail in a database. To understand the full picture, you need to correlate timestamps across logs. Look for the same request ID or timestamp in each service log.

data.title: Key Takeaways
items: Logs are the primary record of server events
Use journalctl for systemd logs with powerful filtering
Application logs are often plain text or JSON
Correlate timestamps across services to trace a request
Start with ERROR level, then check WARN for early symptoms
